# Pronouncing Nnw: a guide for the curious

Saying **Nnw** aloud requires more than reading ​Latin letters on a screen. The conventional spelling is only the entry point into a reconstructed sound and a much older tradition. This post unpacks that sound, the ‌Hieroglyphs evidence, the kindred forms, and the mythological record, then shows how the temple preserves the whole argument without pretending that a diacritic was ever lost.

## At a ‌Glance

- **Restored name:** Nnw
- **ASCII form:** nun
- **Meaning:** "The inert one, waters"
- **Domain of influence:** Primordial Waters
- **Pantheon:** Egyptian
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 𓈗 (Hieroglyphs)

## Overview

**Nnw** ​(*nun*) — The Primeval Waters · The inert one, waters — belongs to the Egyptian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Primordial Waters". The name means ​"The inert one, waters".

**Nnw** — Nun — is not a god of things but of the nothing before things: the dark, inert, life-teeming water that existed before ​creation and surrounds the world still. Every cosmogony begins in him; every temple’s holy lake is his miniature; and every year the Nile’s flood re-stages his one eternal ​act — potential flooding into form.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **Nnw** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/nun/). The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description ​computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *nun* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent ‌citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## The Name

The name is attested in Hieroglyphs as **𓈗**. Etymologically it means "The inert one, waters".

The canonical spelling **Nnw** matches ​the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *nun* contains the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. The editorial work is to fix ​one reviewed reference spelling, preserve capitalization and provenance, and keep the original evidence visible. ‌The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **n** → **N** — Same, capitalized
- **u** → **n** — Special phonetic character
- **n** → **w** — Special phonetic character

## The Original Script

The ​name is preserved in Hieroglyphs as **𓈗** — Egyptian hieroglyphs, attested Egyptian hieroglyphic, c. 3200 BCE – 4th century CE, in Nile Valley, Egypt. The script is written ‌right-to-left / top-to-bottom / multidirectional.

The scholarly transliteration is *Nnw* (Egyptological transliteration), giving the normalized reading Original vocalisation unknown; Egyptological /nuːn/..

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Water ​sign (𓈗) as logogram for the primordial waters
- Full spelling 𓈖𓈖𓏌 adds phonetic complements
- Personification of the pre-creation watery abyss

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is ‌**/nuːn/ (conventional)** — Conventional reading — Egyptian vocalisation not attested.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Nnw** — Written nnw; conventionally vocalised “Nun”. The name is the primeval water itself.
- **** ​— The waters of chaos from which the first mound rose; grammatically masculine here, feminine as Naunet.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “NOON”

Kindred and ​historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Νηῦν (Nēûn) in the cosmogonic doxographies

Every creation cosmogony begins in Nun; every flood-season re-enacts it.

## Mythology

Nun’s mythology is Egypt’s ​creation mythology seen from the water’s side. He never acts — that is his nature, and the meaning of his name, ‘the inert one’ — but everything that ​acts, acts upon or out of him. The creator gods of every temple city are alike in one thing: they stood on Nun’s surface and spoke.

### The Ogdoad ​and the First Mound (Hermopolitan Cosmogony)

At Hermopolis the theology ran: four frog-headed males and four snake-headed females — Nun and Naunet, Huh and Hauhet, Kuk and Kauket, ‌Amun and Amaunet — swam in the primordial water until their inertness ripened into an egg, or a lotus, or the first mound. From that the sun rose. ​Nun heads the eight because water is first among the inert things.

### The Word Upon the Waters (Memphite Theology)

The Shabaka Stone’s Memphite account has Ptah conceiving the ‌world in the heart and speaking it on the primeval waters: creation as a command uttered over Nun. The theology made the water the page and the god’s ​tongue the pen — the deepest Egyptian metaphor for creation as articulation.

### The Sea That Holds the Barque (Solar Books)

In the underworld books the sun’s night barque ‌sails the *Nun* beneath the world — the primeval water is also the water below, the source of renewal. At dawn the barque re-emerges from Nun’s eastern flood: ​every sunrise is a re-creation, every night a return to the uncreated.

### The Inundation as Epiphany (Flood Theology)

The Egyptians called the annual flood simply ‘the arrival’; its ‌waters were Nun revisiting the world, refertilising the mound. Temple holy lakes and the ‘Ocean of the Temple’ pools staged the same theology in architecture: a miniature primeval ​water at the god’s door, in which purity and creation are the same act.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Nnw concentrates in a small set of ‌recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Primeval Water** — The chaos-flood from which the first mound — and every creator — emerged.
- **Bearer of ​the Mound** — He lifts the ben-ben: the primeval hill on which the creator stood to speak the world.
- **The Ogdoad Pair** — With Naunet he heads the ​eight frog- and snake-headed forces of primordial inertness.
- **Surrounding Ocean** — The world floats in him as a bubble in a flood; beyond the horizon, Nun resumes.

## Archaeology ‌& Evidence

The material record for Nnw survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is ‌tied to the name by ancient testimony.

No temple was exclusively Nun’s — water has no address — but every temple carried him: holy lakes, ‘ocean’ basins, and ‌the primeval-mound imagery of the sanctuary floor. The Ogdoad’s frog and snake figures crowd the Late Period faience amulets found across Egypt.

## Across Cultures

Nun is the substrate into which every creator-god’s theology sinks its roots: Atum ‌self-created upon him, Amun hidden within him, Ptah speaking over him. In the late period he was invoked as ‘father of the gods’ while remaining, strictly, no-one’s child. ​Greek cosmologists drew the parallel with their own water-first doxographies — Thales’ ‘all is water’ found its Egyptian precedent in Nun.

Within the Egyptian tradition, closely related names ​in the corpus include [[ab|Ꜣb]], [[akh|Ꜣḫ]], [[amun|Ꜣmun]], [[ankh|ꜥnḫ]], [[anubis|ꜣnpw]], and [[apep|ꜥꜣpp]].

## Cultural Legacy

The image of the world as a bubble of order in an infinite flood passed ‌from Egyptian cosmogony into Hermetic and Gnostic speculation about the deep; and the Nile flood as ‘the return of the uncreated’ remains one of the most quoted ideas in ​Egyptological writing on time and renewal.

## A Meditation

Nun is the shortest name with the ​largest referent in the entire lexicon: the water before names. To write him in ASCII is almost redundant — his element needs no spelling, only sounding. Read the ​name aloud and you have performed his nature: the open vowel, the held *n*, the open vowel again — a breathing in and out, the flood arriving and ​withdrawing.
